title: That you are
hook: a proud son comes home from twelve years of study, his father asks one question, and a line two schools of Hindu thought read two ways
carry: atman and Brahman: one, or two?
tomorrow: the greatest archer alive drops his bow. why?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shankara bowed to the man on the path. Namaste: a bow to the divine in the other. Today, a join at its most serious: the line Shankara's school stands on, read two ways.
screen: `A BOW TO THE DIVINE IN THE OTHER.`

segments.voice: In the Chandogya Upanishad, a boy named Shvetaketu leaves home at twelve to study the Vedas. He comes back at twenty-four, knowing all of them, and very pleased with himself. His father, Uddalaka, watches him walk in and asks one question. Did you ask for the teaching by which the unheard becomes heard, and the unknown known? Shvetaketu has no idea what he means. So the father starts again from the beginning, and his teaching keeps coming back to three words: tat tvam asi. That you are.
screen: `HOME AT TWENTY-FOUR, AND PROUD.` → `DID YOU ASK FOR THE TEACHING?` → `TAT TVAM ASI.`

segments.voice: Here's the join. In the text, the line follows the word atma, the self: sa atma, tat tvam asi. That is the self; that you are. Now, in sandhi, when a long a meets a short a, the two melt into one long a. So atma followed by atat, which means not that, comes out sounding and looking just like atma followed by tat. And two great schools of Hindu thought split it differently. Shankara's school, Advaita, reads tat: that you are. Your deepest self and Brahman, the ground of everything, are one. Their best case: the father says it right after examples where the many dissolve into the one, like salt stirred into water, gone from sight but present in every sip. Madhva's school, Dvaita, offers another split: atat, not that. You are not that. The self and God are truly two, and the self depends on God. Their best case: the self forgets, suffers and needs grace; the ground of everything doesn't, and the letters allow a reading that keeps the two distinct. And this is no grammar quibble. It's one of the deepest questions in Vedanta: is your atman, your deepest self, one with Brahman, or forever distinct and held up by God? For Advaita, the self in the stranger is your own. For Dvaita, everything you have is grace, and the right answer is devotion.
screen: `A LONG A AND A SHORT A MELT.` · `ADVAITA: THAT YOU ARE.` · `DVAITA: NOT THAT.` · `SAME LETTERS, TWO SPLITS.` · then, large: `ATMAN AND BRAHMAN: ONE, OR TWO?`

segments.voice: Write tat tvam asi on paper, and under it, atat tvam asi. Look at the two lines side by side for a few slow breaths. Then think of one person you'll see tomorrow. Try the first line: the same self looking out of their eyes. Then the second: a soul held up by the same God as you. Notice which one changes how you'd treat them.
Sandhi plainly: today, a long a and a short a melting into one, so that that, and not that, can look the same, and atman and Brahman can be read as one, or as two.
Your line: atman and Brahman, one, or two? Shvetaketu's father asked it with three words. Good night.

howItsDone: Tat tvam asi is studied and debated in Vedanta schools; Advaita teachers read it as the identity of the self and Brahman, and Dvaita teachers in Madhva's line read it in ways that keep the self and God distinct.

fork.setup: at dinner, a friend says the Dvaita reading is just a way to dodge tat tvam asi. you lean toward Advaita. what's Dvaita's best case about the self?
options: the letters allow atat, and a self that forgets and needs grace isn't the same as God.
it isn't really a reading; it's a refusal to read the line at all.
it agrees with Advaita completely, just in different words.
fork.reveal: a long a plus a short a melts into one, so the page allows atat. Dvaita reads the self and God as two; Advaita reads them as one. both read the same letters.

original.note: Sanskrit: tat tvam asi, that you are, written joined; Chandogya Upanishad, chapter 6.

trapdoor: what you thought: tat tvam asi has one fixed meaning, and it's only about grammar.
what it means: the same joined letters can be split as that you are, or as not that, you are.
what a scholar hears: ā plus a gives ā (Ashtadhyayi 6.1.101), so sa ātmā tat and sa ātmā atat look alike when joined; Advaita and Dvaita split it differently.

chat.says: Sam asked what tat tvam asi means. i said 'you are that' and dad said 'or not that'?? which is it?
options: both are Hindu: Advaita reads atman and Brahman as one, Dvaita as two, from the same letters.
your dad's joking; the line can only ever mean you are that.
it's just a translation issue, not a real question about the self.
chat.meaning: Uddalaka taught Shvetaketu tat tvam asi. The joined letters split as tat or atat, so Advaita reads the self and Brahman as one and Dvaita as two: one of the deepest questions in Vedanta.

tie.story: Uddalaka answered his proud son Shvetaketu with tat tvam asi, a line whose joined letters can read 'that you are' or 'not that'.
tie.friend: Priya can tell Sam both she and her dad are right: Hindus split this line two ways, as one with Brahman or as two.
tie.you: which reading would change how you treat people?

Uddalaka.meaning: the father and teacher in the Chandogya Upanishad

Advaita.meaning: not two: Shankara's school, self and Brahman as one

Dvaita.meaning: two: Madhva's school, self and God as distinct

Brahman.meaning: in the Upanishads, the ground of everything

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 6.1.1–3 (Shvetaketu leaves at twelve, returns at twenty-four proud; Uddalaka asks about the teaching by which the unheard becomes heard)
Chandogya Upanishad 6.8.7 and following (sa ātmā tat tvam asi, śvetaketo)
Ashtadhyayi 6.1.101 (akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ: like vowels merge into the long vowel)
Shankara's Chandogya Upanishad commentary (tat tvam asi as identity); Madhva's Chandogya commentary and Dvaita readings (including the split sa ātmā atat tvam asi)
